scenes.title: Tryouts
scenes.text:
The sign-up sheet for fall tryouts goes up outside the gym in the second week of ninth grade. A lot of the names on it belong to kids who have played on club teams since elementary school, with private coaches, summer camps, and parents who drive them to tournaments three states away.

There are other ways to play. A club team in the next town holds showcases where college coaches sit in the bleachers with clipboards, if a family can cover the fees, the hotel nights, and the gas. The intramural league at school costs nothing and meets twice a week.

{name} looks at the sheet for a long time.

textVariants.append: {Subj}’s been playing since middle school, and {poss} old teammates are already on the list.
Practice would run until six, and someone would have to pick up the younger kids.

choices.label: {Subj} tries out for the school team
choices.description: No club fees, practice every day after school.

choices.label: {Subj} plays for a club team with college showcases
choices.description: Families earning $100,000 or more spend about {stat:youth_sports_spending_high_income} a year on a child’s main sport.

availability.stretchNote: Young athletes from families earning $100,000 or more are about twice as likely to play club or travel ({stat:travel_club_share_high_income}) as those from families earning under $50,000 ({stat:travel_club_share_low_income}).

choices.authorFlag: Stretch for the two lowest brackets, as at D7. No club price is in the data.
choices.outcome: The schedule is brutal and the team is good. Some weekends there are more college coaches in the stands than parents.

choices.label: {Subj} plays intramural and pickup games
choices.description: Free, twice a week, and nobody keeps stats.
choices.outcome: Tuesday and Thursday nights in the gym, mixed teams, loud and a little chaotic. It’s the best part of {name}’s week.

choices.label: {Subj} skips sports this year
choices.description: More time for school, work, or family.
choices.outcome: {name} gets {poss} afternoons back. Some of them go to homework. Some go to nothing in particular, which also has its uses.

scenes.title: The Roster
scenes.textIfSuccess: The roster goes up on the gym door on Friday afternoon, and {name}’s name is on it, third from the bottom. Practice starts Monday at 3:15. {Subj} wears {poss} new practice jersey around the house all weekend.
scenes.textIfFailure:
The roster goes up on the gym door on Friday afternoon. {name} reads it twice. {Poss} name isn’t there.

A few friends made it. The coach says to come back next year and work on the basics.

scenes.title: Other Ways to Play
scenes.text: Getting cut stings for about a week. Then the question comes back: there are still other ways to play, or {name} can let sports go and use the time for something else.

scenes.title: Friday Night
scenes.text:
Jordan's parents are out of town, and by third period everyone knows it. By lunch the group chat has a playlist. By the last bell somebody's older brother has agreed to "help with supplies," which everyone understands to mean exactly what it sounds like.

{name} has a chemistry test Monday. {Subj} also has a feeling, the kind that only comes at sixteen, that this is one of those nights people will talk about for years, and that {subj}'ll either be in the stories or hear them secondhand.

textVariants.append: Coach has a 7 a.m. practice tomorrow, and he notices who's tired.
{Subj} is on the schedule at the grocery store at 9.

choices.label: {Subj} goes and stays until the end
choices.outcome: {name} gets home at 2:40. It's the best night of the year, and the chemistry test goes about as well as anyone would expect.

choices.label: {Subj} shows up for an hour, then heads home
choices.outcome: {Subj}'s there long enough to be in the photos and home in time to sleep. Nobody remembers that {subj} left.

choices.label: {Subj} stays home tonight
choices.outcome: {Subj} aces the test. On Monday, everyone has an inside joke {subj} doesn't get.

choices.label: {Subj} invites a few friends over instead
choices.outcome: Five friends, two pizzas, a movie nobody watches. It's quieter, and {subj}'ll remember it longer than {subj} expects.

researchNote.title: Who Gets Help Applying
researchNote.text: School counselors help students choose classes, find scholarships, and apply to college. The national average is {stat:counselor_ratio} students per counselor, compared with the {stat:counselor_ratio_recommended} the American School Counselor Association recommends. Families who can pay for private admissions help can make up the difference. Many can't.
